description: Somos estudiantes de ciencias de la computación. Queremos participar en eventos y generar experiencia en entornos reales
summary:
We developed Rescue at the Lunar South Pole, an interactive pixel art web video game designed for children aged 7 to 12. In the story, Dr. Itzel Ramos and her robot Chispa are trapped at the Moon's south pole moments before a solar storm hits, so Mission Control selects the player to lead the rescue mission.

The project addresses the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real space engineering trade-offs into playable game mechanics. Across 12 continuous phases, the player must choose a spacesuit and spacecraft, pack a backpack with a strict 10 kg limit, land under real lunar gravity (1.62 m/s2), drive through frozen craters, and find shelter from radiation using real NASA data (DONKI, OSDR, LRO, and Moon Trek).

It is important because it introduces systems thinking and real space science to children in a free, lightweight game that protects their privacy and shows that in space, no choice is free.

PROJECT DETAILS

What does it do and how does it work?

It is a browser-based narrative adventure divided into 12 sequential missions. A simulation model (simulacion.js) calculates oxygen use, fuel, carried mass, elapsed time, and accumulated radiation dose in real time based on the player's choices and physical parameters. At startup, the system uses an official NASA API key to query NASA DONKI, filtering recent solar activity to select the fastest coronal mass ejection (CME) and calculate when the storm will reach the Moon (with a local backup if offline). At the end, an analytical mission journal explains the impact of every choice and lists all scientific sources used, clearly labeled as Real Data or Example Data.

What benefits does it offer and what is its expected impact?

Educational: It teaches elementary school students evidence-based decision-making, basic physics (lunar gravity, radiation shielding), and critical thinking without overwhelming them with complex terms.

Easy Access: It runs directly in any modern web browser (hosted on GitHub Pages) with no installation, accounts, or powerful hardware required, making it ideal for school computers.

Child Privacy: It is safe by design and never asks for names or personal data; players pick a code name from a preset list.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages and Engine: HTML5, JavaScript (native ES modules), and Phaser 3.80.1, with no transpilers or bundlers needed.

Procedural Graphics and Audio: A 320 x 180 px base canvas scaled 4x using nearest-neighbor interpolation to keep pixel art sharp. Sprites are generated in code from character matrices (pixelart.js) using a palette inspired by PICO-8/Lospec, and sound effects are created in real time with the Web Audio API.

Data and APIs: Official NASA API (api.nasa.gov / DONKI) and separate JSON files (datos.json, textos.json) to keep story text and scientific data independent from the game logic.

Development and Testing: Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub (deployed via GitHub Pages), automated combinatorial balance scripts (pruebas/balance.html) that test all 360 equipment and route combinations, and development assistance from Claude Code.

Instead of using a rigid quiz or simulator, it combines an emotional rescue story—featuring memorable characters like Itzel, Chispa, and the holographic assistant STELLA—with different gameplay mechanics in each phase: a scale and radiation arch in the hangar, thruster-based lunar landing, backpack weight management, driving in permanently shadowed craters at -238 C while cleaning dust and managing a heater, inspecting rover tracks with a magnifying glass, and a book-style final journal with "What if...?" notes.

Game Balance: Through automated testing of 360 scenarios, we made sure there is no single easy winning strategy; every advantage (such as an armored suit or a large spacecraft) has a real cost in mass, agility, or oxygen.

Scientific Integrity: No simulated data is ever presented as real; every value on screen displays its matching source label.

Inclusion and Accessibility: Clear vocabulary adapted for children aged 7 to 12, full support for mouse, keyboard, and touchscreens, a text structure in textos.json ready for translation, and an offline mode (?sinred=1) for schools with limited internet access.
